title: Looping Through a List
objective: Process every item in a list with a for loop, generate a sequence of numbers with range(), and build a new list with a list comprehension.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: A for loop lets you run the same block of code once for every item in a list, without knowing in advance how many items there are. for name in crew: gives you one crew member at a time in name, in order, until the list runs out.

range() generates a sequence of numbers on demand instead of you typing them out. range(3) produces 0, 1, 2; range(1, 4) produces 1, 2, 3, starting at the first number and stopping just before the second. It's most often paired with a for loop when you need to repeat something a set number of times.

A list comprehension builds a new list from an existing one in a single line: [expression for item in list_name]. [n * 2 for n in [1, 2, 3]] produces [2, 4, 6] — it's a compact replacement for a loop that appends to an empty list one item at a time.
explanation.rule: for item in a_list: visits every element in order; range(start, stop) generates numbers up to but not including stop; a list comprehension writes that whole loop-and-append pattern in one line.

examples.title: Visiting Every Item
examples.note: The loop runs once per item in crew, binding member to a different value each pass.

examples.title: range() and a Comprehension
examples.code:
for i in range(1, 4):
    print(f"Round {i}")

squares = [n * n for n in range(1, 5)]
print(squares)
examples.note: range(1, 4) produces 1, 2, 3. The comprehension builds squares in one line instead of looping and appending.

feedback.correct: Correct — range(1, 4) stops just before 4, producing 1, 2, 3.
feedback.incorrect: range()'s stop value is never included. Count from 1 up to, but not through, 4.

checks.question: What does [n * 2 for n in [1, 2, 3]] produce?

feedback.correct: Correct — each item is doubled and collected into a new list.
feedback.incorrect: The expression before 'for' is applied to every item, building a new list from the results.

assignment.title: Training Drill
assignment.brief: Write squad_workout(names) that greets each squad member by name, announces three numbered training rounds, then prints a list of everyone's initials.
requirements: Use a for loop to print "{name} reports for training." for every name in names.
Use range() to print "Round {n} complete." for rounds 1 through 3.
Build a list comprehension that collects the first letter of each name into a list called initials.
Print "Initials:" followed by the initials list.
assignment.starterCode:
def squad_workout(names):
    # Greet each member, announce three rounds, then print initials.
    pass

squad_workout(["Nyx", "Bram", "Odele"])
assignment.testHarness:
# ---- Code Forge validation ----

_cf_buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(_cf_buf):

_cf_result = _cf_buf.getvalue()

Bram reports for training.

Round 1 complete.
Round 2 complete.
Round 3 complete.
Initials: ['N', 'B', 'O']
assignment.outputCheckLabel: squad_workout(["Nyx", "Bram", "Odele"]) prints greetings, rounds, and initials

hints: The first loop is a plain for name in names: printing one line per member.
range(1, 4) gives you 1, 2, and 3 — exactly three rounds, numbered starting at 1.
A list comprehension for this looks like [name[0] for name in names] — name[0] is the first character of each string.
Print the greetings, then the rounds, then the initials line — in that order.
name[0] works on strings the same way indexing works on lists, since a string is a sequence of characters.
